sections.title: The three Japanese writing systems
sections.body: Japanese is written using three systems at once: hiragana (phonetic characters for native Japanese words and grammar), katakana (phonetic characters mostly for foreign-origin words), and kanji (characters borrowed from Chinese, each carrying its own meaning). Hiragana and katakana represent sound only and carry no meaning by themselves; kanji carries meaning and can often be read more than one way depending on context. In everyday writing, all three are mixed together along with romaji (the Roman alphabet) for things like brand names and signage. This book's first job is getting your ear and mouth used to Japanese's sound system before hiragana itself is introduced in Lesson 1 — English uses well over a thousand distinct sounds, while Japanese gets by on a little over a hundred, which is a big part of why Japanese pronunciation is so learnable for English speakers.

points.title: The five vowel sounds
points.explanation: Japanese pronunciation is built on just five vowel sounds, and each one is always pronounced the same way no matter what word it appears in. That consistency is what makes Japanese pronunciation far more predictable than English.

points.title: Lengthened (double) vowels
points.explanation: Some words stretch a vowel sound longer than normal. In this course, a lengthened vowel is always written by repeating the vowel letter rather than using a dash or bar, so the spelling matches how the hiragana will later be written.

points.title: Length changes meaning
points.explanation: Stretching a single vowel can turn one word into a completely different word, so vowel length is never optional or decorative — it has to be pronounced correctly.

points.title: Double consonants
points.explanation: A doubled consonant (written as two of the same letter, like 'kk' or 'tt') is held for a beat longer than a single consonant. Skipping that brief pause can change the meaning of a word entirely.

sections.title: Why some numbers are avoided
sections.body: Four and nine each have two possible readings. One reading of four sounds identical to the word for death, and one reading of nine sounds identical to the word for suffering. Because of that overlap, many buildings skip room or floor numbers containing four or nine, similar to how some Western buildings skip the 13th floor.

points.title: Forming the teens
points.explanation: Numbers 11 through 19 are formed by placing juu (ten) first, followed directly by the single-digit number, the same way Roman numerals stack.

points.title: Forming the tens
points.explanation: Multiples of ten are formed by placing the single-digit number before juu.

points.title: Combining tens and singles
points.explanation: To build a two-digit number that isn't a round ten, string the tens value and the single-digit value together with no extra word in between.

points.title: Hundreds and thousands have irregular readings
points.explanation: Hyaku (hundred) and sen (thousand) sound-shift when combined with certain numbers — for example 300, 600, and 800 change their sound rather than simply attaching san/roku/hachi. These irregular forms have to be memorized rather than derived from a rule.

points.title: Stringing large numbers together
points.explanation: Once the hundreds and thousands are known, any number up to 9,999 can be built by chaining the pieces together in descending order, just like in English.

sections.title: Bowing when you meet someone
sections.body: A bow of roughly 30 degrees, held for a couple of seconds, is standard when meeting someone for the first time. A shallower everyday bow of about 15 degrees is used far more often in daily life. As a learner, you won't be expected to get the depth or timing exactly right, so don't stress over the details early on.

points.title: Introducing yourself politely
points.explanation: Hajimemashite is used only the very first time you meet someone. It's typically followed by stating your name with 'to moushimasu,' a humble way of saying 'I am called ___.'

examples.english: How do you do? I am called Aiko.

points.title: Asking someone's age
points.explanation: Nansai desu ka literally asks 'how many years old are you?' It's a normal question outside of formal business contexts, though it would be considered awkward in a first business meeting.

points.title: Saying your age
points.explanation: Add sai (years old) directly after a number to state an age. A handful of ages have irregular pronunciations that must be memorized rather than derived from the plain number: 1, 8, 9, 10, and 20 all shift in sound.

points.title: Ju- vs Ji- for 'ten' in ages
points.explanation: Ages that are multiples of ten (10, 30, 40, 50...) are officially read with 'ji' rather than 'ju' when combined with sai, even though many people say the 'ju' version casually in speech.

points.title: Guessing someone's age
points.explanation: Nansai ni miemasu ka asks 'how old do I look?' — a common and playful question once you know each other's actual age is a comfortable topic.

notes.title: A more natural way to give your name
notes.body: Many learners are first taught 'Watashi no namae wa ___ desu' (my name is ___), which is grammatically correct but sounds textbook-ish. In everyday conversation, Japanese speakers more commonly just say '___ to moushimasu' or simply state the name followed by desu.

sections.title: Setting up Japanese input
sections.body: Every modern device — phone, tablet, or computer — has a built-in way to add a Japanese keyboard through its language or keyboard settings. Once installed, choosing the 'romaji' input option lets you type using the same alphabet you already know: type the sounds phonetically, watch the hiragana appear as you type, and press the space bar to convert the typed hiragana into kanji if needed, cycling through options with repeated presses. Most devices also offer a quick shortcut (commonly Alt+Shift or a keyboard-switcher icon) to jump between Japanese and English input without digging through settings each time.

sections.title: Adding san to a name
sections.body: Attaching san to the end of someone's name is the everyday way to say Mr., Ms., or Mrs. It's considered impolite to leave it off when referring to someone you're not close to, but you should never attach san to your own name or the names of your own family members.

points.title: No separate plural form
points.explanation: Japanese nouns don't change between singular and plural. A single word like inu can mean 'dog' or 'dogs' depending entirely on context — no article or ending tells you which.

points.title: Making a basic statement with desu
points.explanation: Desu goes at the end of a sentence and roughly means 'is' or 'am,' though the exact English translation depends on context. A single noun followed by desu forms a complete, grammatical sentence.

points.title: Turning a statement into a question with ka
points.explanation: Adding ka to the end of a desu sentence turns it into a yes/no question, functioning like a spoken question mark.

points.title: Asking 'what' with nani / nan
points.explanation: Nani and nan both mean 'what,' but they aren't interchangeable. Nani can stand on its own; nan cannot stand alone and must be paired with another word, most commonly desu.

notes.title: Telling あ (a) and お (o) apart
notes.body: These two characters look similar to new learners. The key difference is the second stroke: あ's second stroke curves, while お's second stroke stays straight until it reaches the loop at the end.

notes.title: Writing direction
notes.body: Japanese is most commonly written left-to-right today, the same direction as English. A top-to-bottom, right-to-left style also exists and is still seen in some books and formal writing, but this course uses the left-to-right style throughout.

sections.title: Sushi vs. sashimi
sections.body: Sushi refers to raw or cooked fish, egg, or vegetables served on vinegared rice, usually with a touch of wasabi between the topping and the rice. Sashimi is simply thin slices of raw fish on their own, without rice.

sections.title: The ko-so-a-do pattern
sections.body: A recurring pattern in Japanese groups words by distance from the speaker: ko- words refer to something close enough to touch, so- words refer to something nearby but out of reach, a- words refer to something far away, and do- words form the question version. This lesson's example is kore/sore/are/dore ('this one'/'that one'/'that one over there'/'which one'), and the same ko-so-a-do pattern will reappear in later lessons with different word sets.

points.title: Marking the topic with wa
points.explanation: Wa marks whatever comes before it as the topic of the sentence, roughly meaning 'speaking of ___' or 'as for ___.' Everything after wa describes or asks about that topic.

examples.english: As for the car, it is red.

points.title: Using wa in questions and answers
points.explanation: Once a topic is marked with wa, you can ask what it is or describe it, and the topic word carries through naturally into the answer.

examples.english: What is the book? (What kind of book is it?)

points.title: dore vs. docchi
points.explanation: Both mean 'which one,' but dore is used when choosing among three or more items, while docchi is used when choosing between exactly two.

examples.english: Which one is the car? (three or more choices)

examples.japanese: ざっしはどっちですか。
examples.english: Which one is the magazine? (two choices)

points.title: Matching the answer's pattern to the question
points.explanation: A natural answer mirrors the grammatical form of the question — if the question used docchi, the answer should stay in the ~cchi family (kocchi/socchi/acchi) rather than switching to kore/sore/are.

examples.japanese: ペンはどっちですか。— こっちです。
examples.romaji: Pen wa docchi desu ka. — Kocchi desu.
examples.english: Which one is the pen? — This one.

points.title: Asking what an unfamiliar word means
points.explanation: You can use the same wa + nan desu ka pattern to ask about a word itself, which is a handy way to build vocabulary in conversation.

examples.japanese: くだものはなんですか。

notes.title: Dropping the topic once it's established
notes.body: Once a topic has been introduced, Japanese speakers typically don't restate it again, unlike English where 'he'/'she'/'it' keeps standing in for it. For example, after saying 'My friend is Kenta,' the following sentences would simply say 'Is 19 years old' and 'Is a student' rather than repeating 'he' each time — the topic stays implied until a new one is introduced.

notes.title: What the dakuten mark does
notes.body: The small double-stroke mark in the upper right of a character (called dakuten) is the only difference between the ka-row (か き く け こ) and the ga-row (が ぎ ぐ げ ご). It changes the consonant sound but the character shape stays the same.

notes.title: Writing が correctly
notes.body: When adding dakuten to か to form が, keep the two dakuten strokes visibly shorter than the character's main strokes — a common mistake is drawing them too large, which makes the character harder to read at a glance.

notes.title: Two acceptable forms of き
notes.body: き is commonly handwritten with its third and fourth strokes joined into one continuous stroke, while printed text usually keeps them as two separate strokes. Both forms are correct and you'll see both in real-world Japanese.

notes.title: Why this course uses spaces
notes.body: Standard Japanese writing doesn't use spaces between words, since kanji naturally shows where words begin and end. Since this course mixes romaji and hiragana before kanji is introduced, spaces are added for readability and will gradually be removed as more kanji is learned.

sections.title: The word boku
sections.body: Boku is a casual word for 'I/me' used almost exclusively by males. It can sound endearing or boyish depending on context. Interestingly, adults will often address an unfamiliar little boy as 'boku' rather than using his name, so a question like 'Boku wa nansai desu ka' addressed to a child means 'How old are you?' — not 'How old am I?'

points.title: The question word dare
points.explanation: Dare works exactly like the other question words you've learned (nan, dore, docchi), but it asks about a person's identity rather than an object.

examples.japanese: だれですか。— せんせいです。
examples.english: Who is it? — It's the teacher.

points.title: Combining wa with dare
points.explanation: Just like any other topic, a person can be marked with wa and then asked about using dare.

examples.japanese: かのじょはだれですか。— ともだちです。
examples.romaji: Kanojo wa dare desu ka. — Tomodachi desu.
examples.english: Who is she? — She's a friend.

points.title: Letting context supply the topic
points.explanation: A sentence like 'Dare desu ka' has no stated topic at all, and that's completely normal in Japanese — the listener is expected to figure out who or what is being asked about from the situation, rather than having it spelled out the way English usually requires.

examples.english: Who is this (person in the photo)?

points.title: Japanese sentences don't usually open with a question word
points.explanation: English happily starts sentences with 'who,' 'what,' or 'which,' but Japanese generally places the question word later in the sentence, after the topic. A direct word-for-word translation from English often sounds unnatural for this reason.

points.title: Starting with a question word using ga
points.explanation: There's an exception to 3-4: when the question word itself needs to be the very first word of the sentence, ga replaces wa as the marker. The answer must then also use ga to stay consistent with the question's pattern.

examples.japanese: だれがせんせいですか。— たなかさんがせんせいです。
examples.romaji: Dare ga sensei desu ka. — Tanaka san ga sensei desu.
examples.english: Who is the teacher? — Tanaka is the teacher.

points.title: Showing possession with no
points.explanation: Attaching no after a word turns it into a possessive, similar to adding 's or using 'mine/yours/his/hers' in English.

examples.japanese: これはだれのですか。— わたしのです。
examples.romaji: Kore wa dare no desu ka. — Watashi no desu.

points.title: Chaining no together
points.explanation: No isn't limited to a single pair of words — you can chain several possessives together to get increasingly specific, working right to left just like in English ('friend's cat's name').

examples.japanese: ともだちのねこのなまえはなんですか。
examples.romaji: Tomodachi no neko no namae wa nan desu ka.
examples.english: What is your friend's cat's name?

notes.title: Two acceptable forms of さ and そ
notes.body: Like き in Lesson 2, さ and そ each have a handwritten form and a printed form that differ slightly in stroke count. Both are correct and legible — pick whichever feels more natural as you practice.

sections.title: Green traffic lights are 'blue'
sections.body: Japanese sometimes groups what English speakers call 'green' under the word for 'blue.' Unripe vegetables and green traffic lights are both described as 'blue' in everyday Japanese, a naming holdover from before the language had a fully separate word for green in common use.

points.title: The particle to (and)
points.explanation: To joins items in a list, placed between every item — it cannot be used to connect whole sentences the way 'and' sometimes does in English.

points.title: Turning a noun into an adjective with no
points.explanation: You already know no as a possessive marker. It has a second job: placed between two nouns, it lets the first noun describe the second, similar to how English stacks nouns together ('coffee cup').

points.title: Using color nouns to describe something
points.explanation: Since the colors in this lesson are introduced as nouns, you need no to use them as descriptions — you can't place a color noun directly in front of another noun without it.

points.title: Six colors also have an i-adjective form
points.explanation: Shiro, kuro, chairo, aka, ao, and kiiro each have an alternate form ending in i (shiroi, kuroi, chairoi, akai, aoi, kiiroi) that can describe a noun directly, with no no required.

points.title: Choosing between the noun and i-adjective forms
points.explanation: When directly describing a noun, either form works and both sound natural. When answering a direct question about color (like 'what color is it?'), the plain noun form is the more natural choice.

examples.english: What color is your cat? — Brown.

notes.title: Writing double consonants with a small tsu
notes.body: A doubled consonant sound is represented by a small つ placed just before the hiragana that gets doubled, and it's kept noticeably smaller than a regular つ so it isn't mistaken for one. For example, がっこう (gakkou, school) uses a small っ right before こ.

notes.title: Why doubled consonants sound different
notes.body: A doubled consonant creates a brief, audible pause right before the consonant sound — skipping that pause is one of the more common pronunciation mistakes beginners make.

notes.title: The rare づ and ぢ
notes.body: ず and じ (from Lesson 3) cover the vast majority of these sounds. づ and ぢ show up in only a small number of words, such as hanaji (nosebleed) and tsuzuku (to continue) — when in doubt, ず/じ is right about 90% of the time.

sections.title: The suffixes kun and chan
sections.body: Kun and chan are affectionate name suffixes, roughly parallel to san but far more casual. Chan is used mostly with girls' names (and often with children generally, regardless of gender), while kun is used mostly with boys' names. Neither should ever be attached to the name of someone above you in social standing — hearing kun or chan is a sign the speaker sees themselves as equal to or higher than the person being addressed.

points.title: Negating i-adjectives
points.explanation: Janai (from Lesson 5) negates nouns, but it cannot negate i-adjectives. To negate an i-adjective, drop the final い and add くない instead.

さむい ／ さむくない

points.title: Wanting and not wanting with hoshii
points.explanation: Hoshii (want) is marked with ga, the same way suki and kirai are. To say you don't want something, apply the i-adjective negation pattern from 6-1: drop い, add くない.

examples.japanese: あたらしいテレビがほしいです。

examples.english: I don't want an old car.

points.title: Reading long chains of no
points.explanation: A sentence with several no's in a row can look intimidating, but each no is just doing the same job — turning what comes before it into a description of what comes after. Read the chain left to right and it unpacks naturally.

examples.japanese: わたしのともだちのけんじさんはにじゅうさんさいです。

points.title: Stating amounts of money
points.explanation: To say an amount of money, attach doru (dollars) or en (yen) directly after the number — no particle is needed in between.

points.title: Counting past 10,000 with the man unit
points.explanation: Japanese counting resets at 10,000 rather than continuing to count in thousands the way English does. Each unit of 10,000 is called man, so 20,000 is 'ni man' (2 units of 10,000), not 'juu ni sen.' This new counting unit takes some adjustment, but it lets you count up to roughly 100 million once combined with what you already know.

notes.title: What the small circle means
notes.body: The pa/pi/pu/pe/po row is made by adding a small circle (handakuten, often just called 'maru') in the same corner where dakuten normally goes. It's written clockwise as the final stroke of the character.

notes.title: Why ふ is romanized as 'fu' rather than 'hu'
notes.body: This course consistently romanizes ふ as fu because the actual sound sits closer to a soft F than an H — a softer, more breathy F than the English F sound.

notes.title: An easier way to write ふ
notes.body: ふ can look intimidating at first, but it becomes much easier if you think of connecting the first two strokes into a shape resembling the number 3.

sections.title: Japanese tea culture
sections.body: Tea is a near-universal part of Japanese hospitality — visiting someone's home often means being offered tea alongside a small snack, frequently a rice cracker called senbei. Despite there being several distinct varieties of green tea (leaf, powdered, roasted), all of them tend to just get called ocha in casual conversation.

notes.title: ii is an exception to the negation pattern
notes.body: Ii and yoi both mean 'good,' but only yoi follows the regular drop-い-add-くない negation rule (yokunai, 'not good'). You may occasionally hear ikunai in casual speech, but it isn't considered standard — stick with yokunai.

points.title: When to use wa vs. ga
points.explanation: This trips up a lot of learners, but it comes down to a handful of consistent rules. (1) Wa can never immediately follow a question word — 'nani wa' is always wrong; it must be 'nani ga.' (2) Ga is the default marker for adjectives like suki/kirai/hoshii, but wa takes over when you're comparing two things or emphasizing a point. (3) Wa and ga can appear in the same sentence together — wa marks the overall topic, ga marks the specific thing being described. (4) Wa is the right choice whenever you're introducing a new topic or returning to one after the conversation moved elsewhere. (5) In casual speech, both particles are sometimes dropped entirely once the meaning is already clear from context.

sections.title: Christmas and holidays in Japan
sections.body: Japan celebrates Christmas, though with its own customs — eating a decorated 'Christmas cake' on Christmas Eve with family, and chicken on Christmas Day, rather than the traditional Western meal. Golden Week, a cluster of consecutive national holidays in early May, is another distinctly Japanese calendar highlight, when many people travel back to their hometowns.

sections.title: Telling apart the 4th and 8th
sections.body: Yokka (4th) and youka (8th) are commonly confused since they sound so similar. One way to keep them straight: the 'yo' in yokka is short, while the 'yo' in youka is stretched longer by the following u — and since 8 is double 4, it makes sense that the '8th' version has the longer sound.

points.title: Forming the months
points.explanation: Japanese months are simply a number followed by gatsu (the reading of the kanji for 'moon/month' in this context). There's no need to memorize twelve unrelated words — just the number-plus-gatsu pattern, with a couple of irregular readings for 4, 7, and 9.

points.title: Making a sentence past tense with deshita
points.explanation: Deshita is the past-tense counterpart of desu, used exactly the same way except it shifts the sentence from 'is/am/are' to 'was/were.'

sections.title: New Year's in Japan
sections.body: New Year's is arguably the single most important holiday period in Japan, comparable to how central Christmas is in the United States. From January 1st through about a week after, much of the country slows down — many shops and companies close so everyone can spend the period with family.

points.title: Saying a year
points.explanation: Nen means 'year.' Attach it after a full number to state a year — and unlike English, Japanese never breaks a year into two-digit chunks (there's no equivalent of saying 'nineteen ninety-eight'); the entire number is read out in full.

points.title: Saying a complete date with the year
points.explanation: A full date always goes year, then month, then day of the month — largest unit of time to smallest, the same ordering principle you already saw with month-then-day in Lesson 8.

points.explanation: Phrases like 'Friday of next week' or 'March of this year' are built by chaining the two time words together with no, always moving from the larger span of time to the smaller one — the same left-to-right logic as any other no chain.

points.title: Asking for something with kudasai
points.explanation: Kudasai works like 'please' when requesting an item, but it can never stand alone — it always attaches to a sentence. The object being requested is marked with を.

points.title: Asking more politely with onegaishimasu
points.explanation: Onegaishimasu also means 'please,' and works the same grammatical way as kudasai (with を marking the object), but it's noticeably more polite. Unlike kudasai, onegaishimasu can also stand completely on its own as a one-word 'please.'

examples.japanese: みずをおねがいします。

points.title: Choosing between kudasai and onegaishimasu
points.explanation: Both are polite and kudasai is perfectly acceptable in everyday situations. Reach for onegaishimasu instead when speaking to someone of higher status, or whenever you want to sound extra polite.

points.title: The particle mo ('too'/'also')
points.explanation: Mo means 'too' or 'also.' When it applies to the sentence's topic, it fully replaces wa or ga rather than being added alongside it.

examples.japanese: バナナがすきです。りんごもすきです。
examples.romaji: Banana ga suki desu. Ringo mo suki desu.
examples.english: I like bananas. I like apples, too.

points.title: A common particle mistake with compliments
points.explanation: Saying 'Kyou wa kirei desu' to compliment someone literally comes across as 'As for today, you're pretty' — implying they aren't pretty on other days, because wa puts emphasis specifically on kyou. Swapping wa for mo fixes it: 'Kyou mo kirei desu' means 'You're pretty today, too,' which is the compliment actually intended.

examples.english: You're pretty today, too. (the safe version)

points.title: Clothing and food sizes
points.explanation: Japanese borrows S, M, and L directly from English for sizes (esu, emu, eru). To use a size word to describe something, turn it into a no-adjective first, the same as any other noun-as-description.

examples.japanese: エルのピザがほしいです。
examples.romaji: Eru no piza ga hoshii desu.

notes.body: When two hiragana combine into one compound sound (like き + ゃ = きゃ), the second character must be written noticeably smaller than the first — writing it full-size changes the meaning into two separate syllables instead of one combined sound.

points.title: Why Japanese has multiple counting systems
points.explanation: Japanese counts different categories of objects with different number words, based on shape or type — round objects, long thin objects, flat objects, and so on. This can feel unusual at first, but English does something similar without thinking about it: 'a slice of pizza,' 'two head of cattle,' 'a flock of birds.' This lesson introduces four of the most commonly used counting systems: a general/abstract counter, a round-object counter, a long-cylindrical-object counter, and a thin-flat-object counter.

points.title: Counters don't take a particle of their own
points.explanation: The object being counted still takes を if it's the object of the sentence, but the counter word itself never takes a particle, no matter which counting system is being used.

points.title: Using ato to mean 'more' or 'else'
points.explanation: Ato means 'more,' 'else,' or 'in addition,' and is placed in front of the item or quantity it refers to. It's fine to follow it with wa.

points.title: Polite vs. informal speech
points.explanation: Polite verb forms are the right default with strangers, in business, or with anyone above you socially. Informal forms are more natural with close friends and family. Until you're comfortable navigating that distinction, staying in polite forms is the safer habit to build.

points.title: How verb conjugation works
points.explanation: Every Japanese verb's dictionary form (the plain, unconjugated form you'd find in a dictionary) ends in a hiragana from the う row — く, る, す, む, and so on. To build the polite form of a regular verb, that final う-row hiragana shifts one column over to the matching い-row hiragana, and one of four endings is attached depending on tense and polarity. Irregular verbs don't follow this shifting pattern and simply have to be memorized.

examples.japanese: かえる → かえります

points.title: Location particles に and へ
points.explanation: Both に and へ can mean 'to' when attached to a destination. に is typically used for an exact destination, while へ leans toward a general direction — though in everyday speech, native speakers mix the two freely. This course defaults to に as the standard choice.

examples.english: I am going to the bank.

points.title: に as a time marker
points.explanation: に also marks a specific point in time, functioning like 'in,' 'on,' or 'at' in English.

examples.japanese: かようびにかえります。

points.title: When to skip the time particle
points.explanation: Relative time words like kyou (today), ashita (tomorrow), senshuu (last week), and rainen (next year) never take に. A simple test: if the English sentence wouldn't use 'in,' 'on,' or 'at' before that time word, don't use に either.

points.title: Verbs come last, and か still makes a question
points.explanation: Just as with desu, verbs always sit at the very end of a Japanese sentence, and adding か after a verb turns the sentence into a question the same way it does after desu.

points.title: The verb わかる takes が
points.explanation: With wakaru (to understand), the thing being understood is marked with が, following the same pattern as suki, kirai, and hoshii.

examples.japanese: にほんごがわかります。

points.title: Building languages and nationalities
points.explanation: Attaching ご to a country name creates the word for that country's language, and attaching じん creates the word for a person of that nationality. A handful of countries don't follow this pattern and have to be memorized as exceptions — most notably America, whose language is simply eigo (English), not 'amerikago.'
